title: Nothing like Him
hook: there is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing (42:11)

segments.voice: Yesterday, signs in the horizons and in themselves, and your line was signs out there, signs in here. Which sign did you catch, outside or in? Today ends the week, and opens Surah Ash-Shura. Day five hundred sixty-seven.

Look around the room you're in. Almost everything comes in pairs or sets. Two shoes. Two hands. Socks, earrings, chairs around a table. Look outside: male and female birds, day and night, hot and cold. Even the things that seem single have a match somewhere, a twin, a counterpart, something they're like. Try to name one thing that has no likeness anywhere. It's harder than it sounds. Surah Ash-Shura, verse eleven, sets up exactly that exercise, and then names the only answer.

Verse eleven begins with creation. The Originator of the heavens and the earth. He made for you mates from among yourselves, and for the cattle, mates. Pairs, everywhere, multiplying. Then, against all those pairs, the line. Pickthall: "Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer." Laysa ka-mithlihi shay'. We met this verse on day two hundred forty-eight, for its last two names. Today, the first half. Look closely at the Arabic. Ka means like. Mithl also means like. Both are there: literally, there is nothing like His like. Grammarians have argued about why. Many say the doubled word is emphasis, like saying nothing, nothing at all, is like Him. Others read it as: there isn't even anything like something like Him. Either way, the sentence closes every door to comparison twice. Surah al-Ikhlas says it in four words. Pickthall: "And there is none comparable unto Him." So everything in the world has a pair, and the One who made the pairs has none. That's why Muslim art in mosques uses calligraphy and pattern instead of pictures of God. And it's why Muslim theologians argued for centuries about how to talk about Allah at all. Different schools drew the lines in different places. But they all start here. Then the verse does something gentle. Right after saying nothing is like Him, it says He hears and He sees. Beyond every picture, and still listening.

The practice: sit with what can't be pictured. Close your eyes. Notice how the mind reaches for an image whenever it thinks of anything: a face, a light, a shape. Let each image come, and gently set it down: not that, not that. Don't try to fill the space with something better. Just rest in the not-picturing. If you pray, you might rest in the verse: nothing is like Him, and He hears. The bell holds the time.
Nothing like Him. Laysa ka-mithlihi shay': in a world made of pairs, the One with no likeness, who still hears and sees. Today's word.

Your line: nothing like him. Today, notice the pairs: shoes, hands, birds, days. Each one is a quiet reminder of the One who has none. Day five hundred sixty-seven, and the end of a week: the Forgiver of sin, the hidden believer, call on Me, repel with better, standing firm, the signs, and the One with no likeness.

howItsDone: Muslims do not make images of God; mosques are decorated with calligraphy and geometric pattern, and 42:11 and Surah al-Ikhlas are central to how Muslim theology speaks about Allah.

fork.setup: the verse has just described creation in pairs: mates for people, mates for cattle. what comes next?
options: and Allah too has a pair.
pairs are the secret of the world.
fork.reveal: nothing is like Him, and He is the Hearer, the Seer: everything has a pair, and its Maker has none.

original.note: Arabic: there is nothing like His likeness, with like said twice (ka, mithl).

trapdoor: what you thought: God is very great.
what it means: in a world where everything has a pair, Allah has no likeness at all, and still hears and sees.

what a scholar hears: the doubled comparison (ka + mithl) is read as emphasis or as negating even a likeness of a likeness; the verse anchors tanzih, while schools of kalam differed on reading the attributes.
